2) Papular urticaria (insect‑bite hypersensitivity) — Commonly causes recurrent, intensely itchy papules on exposed extremities and may persist for months; often clustered and worse on arms/legs.
3) Dermatitis herpetiformis — Intensely pruritic, grouped papulovesicular/papular lesions on extensor surfaces in middle‑aged adults; may be missed if vesicles are not noted and topical steroids are ineffective.
4) Prurigo nodularis (nodular prurigo) — Chronic scratching can produce multiple intensely itchy papules/nodules resistant to topical steroids; consider if lesions are excoriated/lichenified.
5) Eczematous dermatitis / lichen planus variant — Less likely but can present as chronic pruritic papules on extremities; lichen planus often has characteristic violaceous papules and mucosal findings.

Recommended next steps to confirm diagnosis (priority order)
- Immediate focused skin examination including interdigital web spaces and burrows.
- Skin scraping (mineral oil preparation) for scabies mites/eggs/feces — highest yield and rapid.
- If scabies testing negative: consider punch biopsy for histology with direct immunofluorescence (DIF) of a fresh lesion to evaluate for dermatitis herpetiformis; concurrently order serum tissue transglutaminase (tTG IgA) and total IgA.
- CBC with differential (look for eosinophilia) and dermatology referral; consider trial of scabicide (permethrin) if clinical suspicion high while awaiting results.

If you agree, I will request the skin scraping now.
